AGENT INSTRUCTIONS DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your AI coding agent's instruction file still match your repo?

Paste your AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, or copilot-instructions.md and see every file path it references that no longer exists, every npm run script it names that isn't defined in package.json, and known interpreter-mismatch shell footguns — a bare pytest or mypy that can silently resolve to the wrong Python and waste an agent's whole run chasing a phantom failure.

Nothing is uploaded. Pasted text is parsed entirely in this browser. The optional folder picker reads only file names from your chosen folder, never file contents, and nothing leaves your device either way.

1. Paste your instructions file

2. What drifted

KindReferenceDetail

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

node cli.mjs check AGENTS.md                         # resolves refs from the current directory
node cli.mjs check AGENTS.md --root .                 # explicit root
node cli.mjs check CLAUDE.md --package package.json   # explicit package.json
node cli.mjs check AGENTS.md --json                   # machine-readable

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the instructions file, an optional package.json, and the local paths the instructions file itself names: no network call, ever. Exits 1 if anything is found, so it works as a CI gate on the same review that renames a file or a script.

What's checked

CheckHow
Broken file referenceA markdown link target or an inline `code span` that looks like a path (has a slash and a letter-led extension, or is a well-known bare filename like README.md) is resolved against your repo root and flagged if it doesn't exist
Undefined npm scriptnpm run <name>, npm test, and npm start references are checked against your package.json's scripts map, if you supply one
Interpreter-mismatch footgunA bare pytest or mypy inside a fenced code block, without a python3 -m (or python -m) prefix on the same line

Restricted to markdown links and inline code spans on purpose — that is how instruction files actually cite a path when they mean it literally, and scanning ordinary prose for anything path-shaped would flag far more false positives than real drift. A shorthand reference that relies on nearby prose for its directory ("the same validate.py as above") reports as not found even when a longer form of the same path exists elsewhere — a known, disclosed limitation, not a bug. See why these files rot, and where this checker's own edges are, or this checker vs. checking it by hand.

Common questions

Why do AI agent instruction files go stale?

AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are prose, so nothing mechanical keeps them in sync with the repo the way a compiler keeps a type signature in sync with a call site. A script gets renamed, a doc gets moved, a package.json script gets renamed in a refactor -- and the instruction file still points an agent (or a new human contributor) at the old name. The agent then either fails on a command that no longer exists or, worse, silently succeeds against the wrong tool.

What is an interpreter-mismatch footgun?

A bare tool invocation like pytest or mypy that, on a machine where that tool was installed in isolation (a uv tool install, a pipx install), resolves to a different Python interpreter than the one the repository's own dependencies were installed into. The command runs, produces a plausible-looking result (often "module not found"), and is easy to misread as a real failure in the code rather than a wrong interpreter. python3 -m pytest always resolves against the same interpreter as the rest of the repo's tooling.

Does this check whether the instructions are good advice?

No. It never judges tone, completeness, or whether a rule makes sense -- only whether a thing the file points at (a file path, an npm script, a known-bad shell pattern) still matches what the repo actually has today. That is a narrower, purely mechanical question, and it is the one a stale reference actually breaks on.

Is anything uploaded?

No. The browser page parses the text you paste and the file names it reads from a folder you pick entirely in your own browser, and never sends any of it anywhere. It reads only file names from the folder picker, never file contents. The CLI reads only local files -- no network call, ever.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, security, or engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a careful read of your own instruction file. It reports whether a referenced path, script, or known shell pattern matches what it was told about your repo — nothing more, and a clean result is not a guarantee that your instructions are correct or complete. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste and the file names read from a chosen folder are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, folder_selected) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: .env.example Drift Check, Structured Data Drift Check, and License Drift Check ask the same "does the doc still match the code" question about different pairs — an env file, a page's JSON-LD, a dependency tree — with the same deterministic, no-upload shape. Cron DST Drift Check checks a different kind of drift entirely — a cron schedule against the real calendar's daylight-saving transitions. Agent Permission Config Check checks the same AI-coding-agent's config for a different question again — not whether the file still matches the repo, but whether it grants Bash too broadly or leaks a secret in an MCP server's env.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-it-by-hand.html.text:
← back to Agent Instructions Drift Check

This checker vs. checking it by hand

Reading an instructions file and clicking through its links is a normal way to catch drift once, and it works fine for a short file checked right after you edit it. It is a different job from confirming the file is still accurate today, after every commit that touched anything the file names -- most of which nobody thinks to re-check, because they didn't touch the instructions file itself.

Where checking by hand usually goes wrong

StepCommon gap by handWhat this checker does
Confirming every file reference still resolvesClick through the links you remember are there; a file that grew over months has references nobody has looked at in a while, and a rename elsewhere in the repo doesn't prompt anyone to go back and check them.Resolves every markdown link and inline-code path reference against your actual repo in one pass, every time you run it.
Confirming every npm script reference is still definedRun the ones you remember to test; a script renamed in an unrelated refactor a month later silently makes an older reference stale with nothing prompting a re-check.Checks every npm run, npm test, and npm start reference against package.json's scripts map in the same pass.
Spotting a bare pytest or mypyRequires already knowing the specific interpreter-mismatch footgun exists; without that context, a bare tool name and a python3 -m-prefixed one read as interchangeable phrasing during a skim.Flags a bare pytest or mypy in a fenced code block by rule, every time, regardless of whether the reader already knows why it matters.
Re-checking after later, unrelated changesNothing prompts a re-check of a paragraph you didn't just edit -- drift accumulates silently between the checks that do happen.Costs nothing to re-run; wiring the CLI into CI on every PR makes the re-check automatic rather than something to remember.
Is anything I check uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. Runs entirely in your browser; the CLI makes no network call.

Common questions

What's wrong with just opening the file and clicking every link myself?

Nothing, for a short file, checked once. It stops scaling the way these files actually grow: a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md that accumulates dozens of file references and npm-script mentions over months means clicking through all of them, correctly, every time anything else in the repo moves -- and nobody re-checks a paragraph they didn't just edit. This tool resolves every reference in the file the same way, every time you run it, in the time it takes to paste the file in.

I can just run each referenced npm script once to see if it exists -- isn't that enough?

It confirms the scripts that exist today. It does not get re-run the next time a script gets renamed in an unrelated PR, so the instructions file drifts again as soon as you stop checking -- which is exactly when an agent following it hits the stale name. This tool checks every npm run reference against package.json's scripts map in one pass, so re-checking after any change costs nothing extra.

Wouldn't a human reviewer just notice a bare pytest in a code review?

Only if the reviewer already knows the specific footgun exists -- that an isolated tool install (a uv tool install, a pipx install) can put pytest or mypy on PATH pointed at a different interpreter than the repo's own dependencies. Without that context, pytest tests -q and python3 -m pytest tests -q read as interchangeable phrasing, not a real difference, and the one-word gap is easy to skim past even for someone looking. This tool applies the same two rules every time, so it does not depend on the reviewer already knowing the failure mode.

Is anything I check here uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the text you paste and the file names it reads from a folder you pick entirely in your own browser, and never sends any of it anywhere -- exactly like the rest of this tool. The CLI reads only local files, with no network call, ever.

Try it

node cli.mjs check AGENTS.md
node cli.mjs check CLAUDE.md --package package.json

Exits 1 if anything is found, so it works as a CI gate on the same PR that renames a file or a script. See why these files rot, and this checker's own named limits.

This tool reports whether a referenced path, script, or known shell pattern matches what it was told about your repo -- nothing more, and a clean result is not a guarantee that your instructions are correct or complete. It is not legal, security, or engineering advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a careful read of your own instruction file. why-ai-agent-instruction-files-rot.html.text:
← Back to Agent Instructions Drift Check

Why AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files rot

AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, and .github/copilot-instructions.md exist to tell an AI coding agent (or a new human contributor) how a repo actually works: which files to read first, which command runs the tests, which script builds the project. That only stays true while every path, script name, and command it names still matches what the repo actually has — and nothing about how most repos are built keeps that true on its own.

Why it happens: prose, edited on a different schedule than the code it describes

A refactor renames scripts/check.py to scripts/validate.py, or a package.json script gets renamed from lint to lint:fix. The change works, the tests pass, and the PR merges. Updating every instruction file that named the old path or the old script is a manual step no build or type check enforces — the same class of drift as an .env.example falling out of sync with the code that reads it, just with a different reader on the other end.

Why it costs more with an agent reading the file than with a human

A human contributor who hits a broken command in a README usually recognizes the failure for what it is and works around it. An agent following the same instruction can spend an entire turn, or several, treating a wrong command's output as a real signal about the code — the sharpest version of this is the interpreter-mismatch footgun this tool names directly: a bare pytest or mypy that resolves to an isolated interpreter missing the repo's own dependencies reports a plausible-looking "module not found," which reads exactly like a real regression until someone notices which Python actually ran.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

CheckSourceOut of scope for v0
Broken file referenceMarkdown link targets and inline `code spans` that look like a pathBare prose ("the config lives in src"), and fenced code blocks (too noisy — command flags and globs look path-shaped too)
Undefined npm scriptnpm run <name>, npm test, npm startMakefile targets, Python tox/nox sessions, and any script invoked without the literal npm run form
Interpreter-mismatch footgunBare pytest / mypy inside a fenced code block with no python3 -m prefix on the same lineAny other tool with the same shim problem; only the two most commonly documented ones ship in v0

Wiring it into CI as a gate

Run it on every pull request that touches your instruction file or the paths it names:

- name: Check AGENTS.md for drift
  run: node ventures/agent-instructions-drift-check/cli.mjs check AGENTS.md --root .

The command exits non-zero if any file reference is broken, any named npm script is undefined, or a known footgun is present — so the same pull request that renames a file or a script is the one that has to update the instruction file that named it.

Common questions

Isn't this just a markdown link checker?

A general markdown link checker (lychee, markdown-link-check) verifies that a link resolves to a file or URL that exists, which overlaps with this tool's file-reference check. It does not check npm-script references against package.json, and it does not know about the interpreter-mismatch shell footgun this tool looks for -- both specific to the failure modes an AI-coding-agent instruction file actually causes when it goes stale.

Why only markdown links and inline code spans, not all prose?

Because that is how instruction files actually cite a path when they mean it literally -- both this repo's own AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md follow exactly that convention throughout. Scanning ordinary prose for anything path-shaped would flag version numbers, package names, and ordinary sentences far more often than it would catch a real broken reference.

Can it resolve a shorthand reference that relies on nearby prose for its directory?

No, and this is a named limitation rather than a hidden one. A sentence that names a full path once and then refers back to it later with just the filename ("the same validate.py as above") will report the later, shorter reference as not found even though the earlier, fuller path exists. The fix in the instructions file is usually to repeat the full path, which also makes the file easier for a human skimmer to follow.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a referenced path, script, or known shell pattern matches what it was told about your repo — nothing more. It is not legal, security, or engineering advice, and a clean result is not a guarantee that your instructions are correct or complete. Verify by reading the actual files before relying on it.
